entries_new.name: Radio London
entries_new.founder: Don Pierson (Texas) with other investors
entries_new.challenge: UK Parliament, through the 1967 Act that made it illegal to supply or assist unlicensed offshore stations
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast from a ship anchored outside British territorial waters, so that British broadcasting law did not apply at sea.
entries_new.story: Radio London was a pop music station that broadcast to southeast England from the MV Galaxy, a former US Navy minesweeper, anchored in the North Sea about 5.6 km off Frinton-on-Sea, Essex. It ran from 23 December 1964 to 14 August 1967. Its offices were in London's West End. It went off air when the Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967 made it illegal to advertise on, supply or assist unlicensed offshore stations. Several of its disc jockeys later worked for BBC Radio 1.

entries_new.name: Swinging Radio England, Britain Radio and Radio 355
entries_new.founder: Don Pierson (Texas), with William Vick managing the business
entries_new.stopped_by: Closed ahead of the UK Marine Offences law
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast two stations from one ship anchored outside British territorial waters.
entries_new.story: Two stations shared one ship, the MV Olga Patricia, anchored about 7 km off Frinton-on-Sea, Essex. Swinging Radio England played top 40 pop from 3 May to 13 November 1966. Britain Radio played easy listening and was renamed Radio 355 in 1967 under Ted Allbeury, formerly of Radio 390. Management closed Radio England in late 1966 to start a Dutch-language station, Radio Dolfijn, and so avoid the UK law then being drafted. Radio 355 closed at midnight on 5 August 1967.

entries_new.name: Radio Dolfijn
entries_new.founder: William Vick and Jack Curtiss, managers of the Swinging Radio England ship
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast in Dutch from the same offshore ship as Britain Radio, outside UK waters.
entries_new.story: Radio Dolfijn (Radio Dolphin) was a Dutch-language station started in mid-November 1966 by the managers of Swinging Radio England. They closed the English-language station to launch it from the same ship, partly to avoid the British law then about to outlaw offshore stations. The managers had offices and Dutch-speaking disc jockeys set up in Amsterdam. The article names a Dutch counterpart, Radio 227, that joined Radio 355 in a simulcast in July 1967. End date is not given in the sources read.
entries_new.anchor: North Sea off Essex, England (ship position per the Swinging Radio England article)

sources.t: Swinging Radio England (Wikipedia), section on ownership and Radio 355

entries_new.name: Radio Atlanta
entries_new.founder: Allan Crawford, with ship owners Gordon McLendon and Clint Murchison (Texas)
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast from a ship anchored in the North Sea outside British territorial waters.
entries_new.story: Radio Atlanta broadcast pop music from the MV Mi Amigo, anchored 5.6 km off Frinton-on-Sea, Essex, from 12 May to 2 July 1964. The ship had earlier carried the Swedish station Radio Nord. Atlanta started just after Radio Caroline, and the two companies sabotaged each other's fit-out. Audiences and advertising fell short, and Atlanta merged into Caroline, becoming Radio Caroline South. Its Mi Amigo ship went on to carry Caroline broadcasts.

entries_new.name: Commercial Neutral Broadcasting Company
entries_new.founder: Ross Radio Productions Ltd, London (address given for advertisers)
entries_new.mechanism: Hired airtime on the Dutch station Radio Veronica's ship, so English programmes were broadcast from the Dutch side of the North Sea.
entries_new.story: CNBC was an English-language pirate station that rented a few hours each day on Radio Veronica's ship, the Borkum Riff, in 1960 and 1961. Programmes were recorded at Veronica's Amsterdam studio. It is described as the first pirate station to broadcast to the United Kingdom, almost four years before Radio Caroline, though few British listeners heard it because the signal came from the Dutch side of the North Sea. Veronica ended the contract after a few months because Dutch-language programming earned more advertising money.
entries_new.anchor: North Sea off the Dutch coast (approximate; Borkum Riff position not given)

entries_new.name: Radio Atlantis
entries_new.founder: Adriaan van Landschoot (Belgian businessman)
entries_new.stopped_by: Dutch Marine Offences Act, in force 1 September 1974
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast Flemish and English programmes from ships off the Dutch and Belgian coast.
entries_new.story: Radio Atlantis was a Belgian-owned station that began on 15 July 1973 aboard Radio Caroline's MV Mi Amigo. Its owner ran a chain of clothing and record companies called Carnaby and wanted advertising he could not buy on Belgian state radio. After the Caroline contract ended in October 1973, it bought its own ship, the MS Janine, and resumed on 30 December 1973. It closed on 31 August 1974, the day before the Dutch Marine Offences Act took effect.
entries_new.anchor: North Sea off the Netherlands and Belgium (approximate)

entries_new.name: Radio Delmare
entries_new.founder: Gerard van Dam
entries_new.stopped_by: Dutch Radio Control Office raid, then a stranding of the ship
entries_new.mechanism: Tried to restart Dutch offshore broadcasting from a ship at sea after the closure of Radio Veronica and Radio North Sea International.
entries_new.story: Radio Delmare was a Dutch offshore station led by Gerard van Dam. The Dutch Radio Control Office and police boarded its ship, the MV Aegir, at The Hague on 23 June 1978 and disabled it. The crew slipped away, moved the ship out and started broadcasting. The Aegir ran aground on 11 September 1978 when its improvised anchor failed. A 1979 attempt from the MV Martina ended after three weeks.

entries_new.name: Radio Monique
entries_new.founder: Fred Bolland (Dutch businessman), leasing a transmitter from Ronan O'Rahilly of Radio Caroline
entries_new.mechanism: Leased the 50 kW transmitter on the Radio Caroline ship Ross Revenge to broadcast to the Netherlands and Belgium.
entries_new.story: Radio Monique broadcast to the Netherlands and Belgium from the Radio Caroline ship MV Ross Revenge. In December 1984 Caroline's owner leased its 50 kW transmitter to Fred Bolland, who started the station on 16 December and named it after his ex-wife. It had a high turnover of disc jockeys. It was sold in October 1987 and moved to 819 kHz. A successor, Radio 558, later Radio 819, started in May 1988. Bolland and former staff returned in 2020 from land, on AM 918 kHz.
entries_new.anchor: North Sea off the Netherlands and Essex (approximate)

entries_new.name: Arutz Sheva offshore radio
entries_new.founder: Rabbi Zalman Baruch Melamed
entries_new.stopped_by: Israeli courts and prosecutions; the station ended radio operations in 2003
entries_new.challenge: Israeli prosecutors; the Supreme Court of Israel voided a 1999 law that would have licensed it
entries_new.mechanism: Generated its broadcast on the MV Eretz HaTzvi in the Mediterranean and aired it into Israel.
entries_new.story: Arutz Sheva, a station identifying with religious Zionism, began in 1988 and broadcast from the MV Eretz HaTzvi in the Mediterranean, with a base at Beit El. In 1999 the Knesset passed a law licensing it and excusing earlier illegal broadcasting; the Supreme Court of Israel voided the law in March 2002. In October 2003, ten employees were convicted of running an illegal station in 1995 to 1998, partly from Israeli waters. Its radio operations ended in 2003. It continues as a news website.

entries_new.name: Radio Hauraki
entries_new.founder: David Gapes, Derek Lowe, Ian Magan, Chris Parkinson and Denis O'Callahan
entries_new.stopped_by: New Zealand ended the state radio monopoly in 1970
entries_new.challenge: New Zealand Broadcasting Corporation and the Marine Department
entries_new.recognition: Licensed to broadcast on land by New Zealand in 1970
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast from the vessel Tiri anchored beyond the 3-mile territorial limit in the Hauraki Gulf, outside the state broadcasting monopoly.
entries_new.story: Radio Hauraki was started by five men to break the New Zealand state monopoly on radio. Its vessel Tiri anchored outside the 3-mile limit in the Hauraki Gulf in late 1966. The Tiri ran aground on Great Barrier Island on 28 January 1968, and the Kapuni, renamed Tiri II, replaced it. In mid-1970 the state allowed Hauraki to broadcast legally on land, after 1,111 days at sea. Announcer Rick Grant was lost overboard on the final voyage. It is now a national network.

entries_new.name: USCGC Courier (Voice of America ship)
entries_new.founder: US Department of State and US Coast Guard
entries_new.mechanism: A US government ship with a 150-kilowatt transmitter, stationed off Rhodes to relay Voice of America programmes toward Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union.
entries_new.story: The Courier was a US Coast Guard cutter fitted as a floating relay station for Voice of America under Operation Vagabond, announced in April 1951. It carried a 150-kilowatt medium-wave transmitter and two 35-kilowatt shortwave units. From 17 July 1952 to 13 August 1964 it was stationed off Rhodes, Greece, and spent no time in US waters. The Soviet Union was jamming parts of the VOA network at the time. It was decommissioned in 1964 and scrapped in 1977.

entries_new.name: Man-in-the-Sea
entries_new.founder: Edwin A. Link; aquanauts Robert Sténuit and Jon Lindbergh
entries_new.mechanism: Divers lived under pressure in a steel cylinder or an inflatable dwelling lowered to the seabed.
entries_new.story: Man-in-the-Sea was a diving project led by Edwin A. Link. On 6 September 1962 Robert Sténuit spent 24 hours 15 minutes at 61 metres in a steel cylinder, becoming the first aquanaut. In June 1964 he and Jon Lindbergh spent 49 hours at 126 metres in Man-in-the-Sea II, living in a submerged portable inflatable dwelling (SPID). The aim was to test how the body copes with long stays under pressure, and no territorial claim was made. The pin marks no verified site; the source gives none.
entries_new.anchor: Site not given in the source

entries_new.name: BAH I
entries_new.founder: Biologische Anstalt Helgoland
entries_new.mechanism: A 6 m by 2 m steel habitat holding two divers, used in the Baltic Sea and Lake Constance.
entries_new.story: BAH 1, named for the Biological Institute Helgoland, was a 6 m long, 2 m wide, 20 tonne habitat for two people. Its first mission in September 1968 put two divers at 10 m depth in the Baltic Sea for 11 days. In June 1969 an attempt to anchor it at 47 m in Lake Constance flooded it with two divers inside, and it sank to the seabed. They were raised on the decompression schedule and were not harmed. It is displayed at the Nautineum in Stralsund.

entries_new.name: Edalhab
aka: Engineering Design and Analysis Laboratory Habitat
entries_new.founder: Students of the Engineering Design and Analysis Laboratory (US)
entries_new.cost: $20,000 (about $187,000 in today's money, per the source)
entries_new.mechanism: A student-built cylinder placed on the bottom of Alton Bay and later off Miami.
entries_new.story: Edalhab was a horizontal cylinder 2.6 m high and 3.3 m long, weighing 14 tonnes, built by students for about $20,000. From 26 April 1968 four students spent 48 hours 6 minutes in it in Alton Bay, New Hampshire. Two more missions followed at 12.2 m. In 1972 it was used in three Florida Aquanaut Research Expedition missions off Miami at 13.7 m, with the University of New Hampshire and NOAA, breathing nitrox. The conversion raised its weight to 23 tonnes.

entries_new.name: Bentos-300
entries_new.founder: Soviet Union
entries_new.mechanism: A manoeuvrable submersible with a diver lock-out chamber that could rest on the seabed for two weeks.
entries_new.story: Bentos-300 was a Soviet manoeuvrable submersible with a lock-out for divers, able to sit on the seabed at up to 300 m for two weeks with about 25 people aboard. It was announced in 1966 and first deployed in 1977; two vessels were planned. It sank in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in 1992. Several attempts to recover it failed, and it was cut up and removed for scrap between November 2011 and the following six months.

entries_new.name: MarineLab
aka: Midshipman Engineered & Designed Undersea Systems Apparatus
entries_new.founder: US Naval Academy ocean engineering programme (Dr. Neil T. Monney); later Marine Resources Development Foundation
entries_new.mechanism: A shore-supported habitat in a mangrove lagoon at Key Largo, run by a foundation inside a US state park area.
entries_new.story: MarineLab began in 1973 as MEDUSA, a US Naval Academy student project. It was donated to the Marine Resources Development Foundation in 1983, placed in John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Key Largo, in 1984, and moved to a mangrove lagoon in 1985. It housed three or four people. NASA used it in 1993 to 1995 for life-support studies. It is described as the longest-serving seafloor habitat, operating from 1984 to 2018, and is now on display at the foundation.

entries_new.name: Scott Carpenter Space Analog Station
entries_new.founder: NASA (designed by engineer Dennis Chamberland)
entries_new.mechanism: A NASA training habitat set near Key Largo to study undersea and space living side by side.
entries_new.story: The Scott Carpenter Space Analog Station was a NASA project near Key Largo, Florida, run on six-week missions in 1997 and 1998. It showed what undersea and space missions have in common in science and engineering. About 20 aquanauts rotated through it, including NASA scientists and engineers and film director James Cameron. NASA engineer Dennis Chamberland designed it.

entries_new.name: Galathée
entries_new.founder: Jacques Rougerie (French architect)
entries_new.mechanism: A semi-mobile habitat-laboratory moored in the water column at any depth from 9 to 60 metres.
entries_new.story: Galathée was the first underwater habitat built by French architect Jacques Rougerie, launched on 4 August 1977. Its feature is that it is semi-mobile and can be moored at any depth between 9 and 60 metres, so it can be added to the marine environment in phases with limited impact on the ecosystem. Rougerie lived in it himself. The source gives no site, so the pin marks nothing verified.
entries_new.anchor: Site not given in the source

entries_new.name: Aquabulle and Hippocampe
entries_new.founder: Jacques Rougerie (French architect)
entries_new.mechanism: Small shelters suspended in midwater rather than resting on the seabed.
entries_new.story: Jacques Rougerie launched the Aquabulle in March 1978, a shelter 2.8 m high and 2.5 m wide hung in midwater between 0 and 60 m, holding three people for several hours. A series was later built and some are still used by laboratories. In 1981 he launched Hippocampe, a scientific base suspended in midwater in the same way, for two people on saturation dives to 12 m for 7 to 15 days. It was also designed as an undersea logistics base for the offshore industry.
entries_new.anchor: Site not given in the source

entries_new.name: Progetto Abissi
aka: La Casa in Fondo al Mare
The House at the Bottom of the Sea
entries_new.founder: Explorer Team Pellicano (Italian diving team)
entries_new.mechanism: Three cylindrical chambers on the seabed serving as the set of a television game show.
entries_new.story: Progetto Abissi, also called La Casa in Fondo al Mare (The House at the Bottom of the Sea), is an Italian habitat designed by the diving team Explorer Team Pellicano. It has three cylindrical chambers and served as a platform for a television game show. It was first deployed in September 2005 for ten days, and in 2007 six aquanauts lived in the complex for 14 days. The source gives no location.
entries_new.anchor: Site not given in the source

entries_new.name: Lloyd Godson's Biosub
entries_new.founder: Lloyd Godson, for an Australian Geographic competition
entries_new.mechanism: A self-supplying underwater habitat that made its own power, water and air.
entries_new.story: The Biosub was an underwater habitat built in 2007 by Lloyd Godson for a competition run by Australian Geographic. It generated its own electricity from a bicycle, made its water with an Air2Water Dragon Fly M18 unit, and produced its oxygen from algae grown in a Biocoil from a Cascade High School biology class. Trygons Designs built the habitat shell. The source gives no location.
entries_new.anchor: Site not given in the source

entries_new.name: Ithaa undersea restaurant
entries_new.founder: Conrad Maldives Rangali Island hotel; built by M.J. Murphy Ltd
entries_new.mechanism: A glazed restaurant reached by a corridor from the hotel and open to the atmosphere, so no compression is needed.
entries_new.story: Ithaa (Dhivehi for mother of pearl) is described as the world's only fully glazed underwater restaurant, at the Conrad Maldives Rangali Island hotel. Guests reach it by a corridor from above the water, and it is open to the atmosphere, so no compression or decompression is needed. M.J. Murphy Ltd built it, and its unballasted mass is 175 tonnes. It is a hotel facility inside Maldivian waters, with no claim of separate status.

entries_new.name: Red Sea Star
entries_new.mechanism: An underwater restaurant with three modules, reached from the shore, with its dining room 6 m below the surface.
entries_new.story: The Red Sea Star in Eilat, Israel, had three modules: an entrance above the water, a restaurant with 62 panorama windows 6 m under water, and a ballast area below. The whole construction weighed about 6,000 tonnes and seated 105 people. It shut down in 2012. It stood in Israeli waters of the Gulf of Aqaba as a commercial attraction.

entries_new.name: Coral World Underwater Observatory
entries_new.mechanism: An observation chamber about 12 m down, reached by footbridge from shore and a shaft from above the water.
entries_new.story: The first part of Coral World Underwater Observatory in Eilat was built in 1975. A second underwater observatory joined it by tunnel in 1991. Visitors reach the complex by a footbridge from the shore and a shaft from above the water, and the viewing area lies at about 12 m depth.

entries_new.name: Ichthyander Project
entries_new.founder: Members of the amateur diving club Ichthyander, Donetsk
entries_new.stopped_by: The club was ordered dissolved after the 1967 expedition; the project was discontinued
entries_new.mechanism: Amateur divers built a seabed habitat off Cape Tarkhankut, then tried to move to state-backed research.
entries_new.story: The Ichthyander Project was the first Soviet underwater habitat project, begun in the 1960s by an amateur diving club in Donetsk. At Cape Tarkhankut in Crimea, one person spent three days continuously underwater in August 1966, and the habitat ran for two weeks in 1967. A later attempt to put the work under state support failed and the project ended. It preceded other early Soviet habitats such as Sadko, Chernomor and Sprut. Cape Tarkhankut is in Crimea, which Russia controls and Ukraine claims.

entries_new.name: Jounieh Floating Island project
entries_new.challenge: Local officials, over environmental and regulatory concerns
entries_new.mechanism: A floating island with a luxury hotel proposed in Lebanese coastal waters, needing local permission.
entries_new.story: The Jounieh Floating Island project was a proposal to build a floating island with a luxury hotel at Jounieh, north of Beirut, Lebanon. Local officials raised environmental and regulatory concerns, and the project had stalled by 2015. It would have sat in Lebanese coastal waters and under Lebanese rules, so it did not aim to create a separate territory.

entries_new.name: Dogen City
entries_new.founder: N-Ark (Japanese consortium)
entries_new.mechanism: A floating city built as a healthcare centre, with construction hoped to begin by 2030.
entries_new.story: Dogen City is a proposal by a Japanese consortium called N-Ark to build a floating healthcare city for 10,000 people. The consortium hopes to start construction by 2030. The source gives no site, so the pin marks Japan generally, where the consortium is based.

entries_new.name: Spiral Island and Joyxee Island
entries_new.founder: Richart "Reishee" Sowa (British artist)
entries_new.stopped_by: Hurricane Emily (2005) destroyed the first island; local authorities ordered the second removed in January 2019
entries_new.challenge: Port and local authorities in Mexico
entries_new.mechanism: Built a floating island from plastic bottles in sheltered Mexican waters.
entries_new.story: British artist Richart Sowa built Spiral Island from about 250,000 plastic bottles in nets, topped with plywood, bamboo, sand and mangroves. It was 20 by 16 metres, in a lagoon near Puerto Aventuras, Mexico, from 1998. He was ordered out of the canal in 2004 and port authorities let him tow it, but Hurricane Emily destroyed it in 2005. Joyxee Island, its replacement near Isla Mujeres, opened for tours in 2008 and was removed on local orders in January 2019.

entries_new.name: Utopia residential ocean liner
entries_new.founder: Utopia Residences, financed largely by the Frontier Group
entries_new.mechanism: Planned to sell 190 residences on a 296 m ship built by Samsung Heavy Industries.
entries_new.story: Utopia is a planned residential ocean liner. The plan was for a 296 m, 108,000 tonne ship with 190 residences and a 175-room hotel, built by Samsung Heavy Industries for a reported US$1.1 billion. Prices rose from US$3.9 to 30 million to US$36 million by 2018. The shipbuilding contract was suspended in 2014 for lack of funds, and a 2017 letter of intent set delivery for 2022. The source lists it as planned, not built.
entries_new.anchor: South Korea (planned shipbuilder's country; no site given)

entries_new.name: RXKR
entries_new.founder: Operators of the SS City of Panama
entries_new.stopped_by: Shut down at the request of the US Department of State
entries_new.challenge: US Department of State; the Panamanian government was reportedly misled about the purpose
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast pop music and advertisements from a ship anchored off California, described to Panama as a tourism promotion.
entries_new.story: RXKR was the first station to broadcast to the United States from international waters. It ran from May to August 1933 aboard the SS City of Panama, a cargo carrier anchored off California that was supposed to advertise tourism in Panama to Americans. The operators instead broadcast popular music and advertisements, which the source says fooled the Panamanian government. The US Department of State asked for the station to be shut down, and it closed in August 1933.
entries_new.anchor: Off southern California, USA (approximate; exact position not given)

entries_new.name: Radio Free America (Carl McIntire)
entries_new.founder: Dr. Carl McIntire
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast religious programmes from a ship anchored off New Jersey, outside US waters.
entries_new.story: Radio Free America was a short-lived religious station run by Dr. Carl McIntire in 1973. It broadcast from the MV Columbus, anchored off the coast of New Jersey, USA. It is one of three stations the Wikipedia article on pirate radio in North America lists as broadcasting from international waters, with RXKR in 1933 and Radio Newyork International in 1987 to 1988. The sources read give no end date or cause of closure.
entries_new.anchor: Off New Jersey, USA (approximate; exact position not given)

entries_new.name: Radio Newyork International
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast from a ship anchored off Jones Beach, Long Island.
entries_new.story: Radio Newyork International was a station that broadcast from a ship anchored off Jones Beach, Long Island, New York, in 1987 and 1988. The Wikipedia article on pirate radio in North America lists it as one of three stations that broadcast from international waters, after RXKR in 1933 and Radio Free America in 1973. The sources read do not say who ran it or how it ended.
entries_new.anchor: Off Jones Beach, Long Island, New York, USA (approximate)

entries_new.name: Capital Radio (MV King David)
entries_new.mechanism: Broadcast to the Netherlands from the ship King David at sea.
entries_new.story: Capital Radio was a station that broadcast to the Netherlands in 1970 from the MV King David. The Wikipedia article on pirate radio in Europe lists it among the Dutch-targeted offshore stations, with Radio Delmare in 1978, Radio Monique from 1984 to 1987 and Radio 558/819 from 1988 to 1989. The sources read give no further detail on its ship position or how it ended.

entries_new.name: SeaOrbiter
entries_new.founder: Jacques Rougerie, with Jacques Piccard and Jean-Loup Chrétien (Floating oceanographic laboratory organisation)
entries_new.mechanism: A vertical, drifting research vessel designed to drift with ocean currents, with a pressurised deck for divers.
entries_new.story: SeaOrbiter is a proposed ocean research vessel based on ideas of the French architect Jacques Rougerie. It would be a 1,000 tonne semi-submersible, 51 m tall with 31 m below the surface, floating vertically and drifting with the currents. Living quarters and laboratories would sit under the surface, with a pressurised deck for divers. Construction was due to start in 2014, but by May 2015 only its Eye section was complete, and the source reports no other construction as of 2024.
